title: An Ode to Jurisprudential Disruption
keywords: Van Dorn to Manalo foreign divorce
Howard Calleja Bongbong Marcos Leni Robredo

primary_topics: Foreword to the Ateneo Law Journal (date: August 1, 2018) -- written at the request of Lead Editor Angelo Francesco F. Herbosa
The 'disruptive symphony' thesis: the 10 articles in the volume appear disparate but are united by a single arching theme -- disruption of existing jurisprudence, systems and norms

CJP's extended commentary on seven of the ten articles: Diokno (judicial/legal reforms), Candelaria-Balisong (Republic v. Sereno), Santiago-Pelongco (same), Sta. Maria (foreign divorce from Van Dorn to Manalo), Calleja (Marcos v. Robredo shading threshold), Mata-Perez (TRAIN 1), and the technology trio (WTO, online child exploitation, Data Privacy Act)

The forward-looking question on Republic v. Sereno: when Court composition changes and most incumbents retire, will the quo warranto ouster decision withstand a petition declaring it void for lack of due process and biased majority? Could Sereno be returned to her post as first female Chief Justice?
sub_topics: The 'disruptive symphony' construct: at first blush the 10 articles 'appeared to be unrelated and disparate, producing a cacophony of voices without any uniting melody'; on closer look, 'their very disparateness and seeming disunity as the arching melody itself'; unity in diversity of law

Article 1 -- Diokno ('Now or Never: Judicial and Legal Reforms in the Philippines'): disrupts the present state of jurisprudence and judiciary; traces how justice system was 'robbed of its independence and integrity by an unwanted dictatorship'; procedural rules 'borrowed rather sketchily from the American jury system and imbedded into our judiciary bereft of juries'; Diokno offered solutions and remedies

Article 2 -- Candelaria-Balisong on Republic v. Sereno: treated mostly as the SC's way of 'cleansing itself of what it... considered as the void ab initio ascension of its Primus Inter Pares'; the Court 'consolidated its power to exact accountability even from its own leader'

Article 9 -- Santiago-Pelongco on Republic v. Sereno (revisiting constitutional qualifications): read together with Candelaria-Balisong; dissects ponencia and opinions; addresses 'apparent misuse of a remedy found only in the Rules of Court to undermine a constitutional remedy... historically intended as the only method to oust impeachable officials'

CJP's Sereno forward-look: when Court composition changes -- 'which is not remote since most of the incumbent justices would be retiring in the next few years' -- will the decision withstand a petition declaring it void for 'being rendered without due process by a biased majority who apparently had not only prejudged their Chief but in fact conceived the very weapon of quo warranto to oust her'? Could Sereno be returned as first female CJ?

Article (Van Dorn to Manalo) -- Sta. Maria on foreign divorce in mixed marriages: Article 26 paragraph 2 of Family Code 'has been zigzagged by the Supreme Court, in the process succumbing to judicial legislation in the guise of interpretation'; latest jurisprudence: Republic v. Manalo (April 24, 2018), 'dissected severely by the author'
Article on IP -- Negre-Kaufman: 'clear allusion to comparable decisions of the Scotus that may be applicable in the Philippine setting'; CJP declines further comment
Article 'tale of two shades' -- Calleja on Marcos v. Robredo: which shading threshold (50% or 25%) should be used in revising contested ballots in Bongbong Marcos' protest vs VP Leni Robredo

Article -- Mata-Perez on TRAIN 1: CJP raises a counter-question: 'Why is the government -- in the guise of pursuing its Build, Build, Build program -- raising new revenue streams when the new infrastructures it desires could be constructed without imposing new taxes through the current Public-Private Partnership (PPP) agreements?'

Technology trio: WTO article (Baguilat), online sexual exploitation of children (Aritao-Pangilinan), Data Privacy Act (Pardu-Jacob); together they 'examine quite fittingly the most disruptive phenomenon of our time: technology'

Technology's disruption of privacy: the right to privacy is 'not expressly provided in the Constitution but inherently imbedded in it'; disrupted by the Internet and its three advanced derivatives: AI, Blockchain Technology, and Internet of Things

CJP's call: 'law, lawmakers, magistrates and lawyers must keep pace with the speedy march of science, if they must maintain the balance between the right to privacy and the utter indispensability of transparency to promote good governance'

Closing tribute: 'potential great lawyers they are who write and edit, and those who verbalize and moot'; the Philippines combines solicitors and barristers into singular attorneys capable of becoming judges, justices, lawmakers and implementers; Herbosa's team as future 'topnotch advocates and eminent justices'

stances.claim: The Republic v. Sereno quo warranto ouster decision -- voted 8-6 -- was rendered 'without due process by a biased majority who apparently had not only prejudged their Chief but in fact conceived the very weapon of quo warranto to oust her.' When the Court's composition changes and most incumbents retire, the decision may not withstand a petition declaring it void -- possibly enabling Sereno's return to her post as first female Chief Justice. CJP deliberately leaves this as a question for the academe.
stances.rhetorical_move: future-reversal question: posing the constitutional challenge to the Sereno ouster as a contingent future question, not a current demand -- protecting himself from charges of direct advocacy while making the legal point
stances.confidence: asserted as a prospective legal analysis, framed as a question for the academe

stances.claim: The 'Build, Build, Build' program should be financed through Public-Private Partnership agreements rather than through new tax revenue streams. Raising new taxes through TRAIN 1 for infrastructure is unnecessary when PPP agreements can achieve the same result. This is CJP's rare policy critique embedded in a law journal foreword.
stances.rhetorical_move: policy-counter-question: the PPP-vs-new-taxes argument as CJP's one normative policy intervention in an otherwise analytical Foreword
stances.confidence: asserted as a 'raise a counter-question' observation, not a firm conclusion

stances.claim: The 10 apparently disparate articles in the volume are united by a single arching theme: disruption -- specifically, the 'disruptive symphony of legalities, or more commonly, unity in diversity of law.' The Foreword's intellectual contribution is precisely this reframing of apparent cacophony as an emergent unity.
stances.rhetorical_move: meta-analytical synthesis: elevating the Foreword from an introduction to a thematic interpretive claim about the volume as a whole
stances.confidence: asserted as CJP's original analytical contribution to the volume

notable_anecdotes: The Sereno future-reversal question: 'When the composition of the Court would have changed... will the decision withstand a petition to declare it void on the ground that it was rendered without due process by a biased majority who apparently had not only prejudged their Chief but in fact conceived the very weapon of quo warranto to oust her? If such a time and reversal would ever come, would Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno be returned to her post with the distinction of being the first woman to head the highest court of the land?'

The PPP counter-question for TRAIN 1: 'Why is the government -- in the guise of pursuing its Build, Build, Build program -- raising new revenue streams when the new infrastructures it desires could be constructed without imposing new taxes through the current Public-Private Partnership (PPP) agreements?' -- CJP's sole policy intervention embedded in an otherwise analytical foreword.

The Diokno-writing-for-Ateneo irony: the first article, by Jose Manuel Diokno (the 'intrepid dean of De La Salle College of Law'), disrupts the existing order by being published in the law journal of rival Ateneo -- the disruption theme embodied in the authorship itself.

The solicitor/barrister observation: 'The Philippines and the United States combined them [solicitors and barristers] into singular attorneys capable of becoming judges, justices, lawmakers and implementers. To them surely belong Herbosa and his team of editors and writers.' -- the closing tribute to the journal's editors.

one_paragraph_summary: Written August 1, 2018 as the Foreword to the Ateneo Law Journal at the request of Lead Editor Angelo Francesco F. Herbosa, this piece by CJP advances the 'disruptive symphony' thesis: the volume's 10 apparently disparate articles are united by a single arching theme -- disruption -- with their very disparateness as 'the arching melody itself.' He comments on seven articles: Diokno's ('Now or Never') traces how the justice system was 'robbed of its independence and integrity by an unwanted dictatorship' and offers reform solutions; Candelaria-Balisong on Republic v. Sereno treats it as the Court 'consolidating its power to exact accountability even from its own leader'; Santiago-Pelongco (to be read together with Candelaria-Balisong) dissects the ponencia's 'apparent misuse of a remedy found only in the Rules of Court to undermine a constitutional remedy historically intended as the only method to oust impeachable officials.' CJP's sharpest intervention is his forward-looking question on Sereno: when the Court's composition changes and most incumbents retire, will the decision withstand a petition declaring it void for 'being rendered without due process by a biased majority who apparently had not only prejudged their Chief but in fact conceived the very weapon of quo warranto to oust her?' -- potentially enabling Sereno's return as 'the first woman to head the highest court of the land.' Sta. Maria's foreign divorce article (Van Dorn to Manalo) exposes Article 26 of the Family Code as 'zigzagged by the Supreme Court, in the process succumbing to judicial legislation in the guise of interpretation'; Calleja tackles the Marcos v. Robredo 50%-vs-25% shading threshold; Mata-Perez on TRAIN 1 prompts CJP's sole policy intervention: 'Why is the government raising new revenue streams when infrastructure could be built through PPP agreements?' The technology trio -- WTO (Baguilat), online child exploitation (Aritao-Pangilinan), Data Privacy Act (Pardu-Jacob) -- is praised as examining 'the most disruptive phenomenon of our time: technology,' prompting CJP's call that 'law, lawmakers, magistrates and lawyers must keep pace with the speedy march of science.' He closes by honoring Herbosa's team as future 'topnotch advocates and eminent justices': 'My wish is to live long enough to witness their passage.'
